title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 4: Service Level Objectives (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## SLI, SLO, SLA definitions

A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided. Common SLIs include request latency, error rate, system throughput, availability, and durability. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI, typically structured as SLI less than or equal to target, or lower bound less than or equal to SLI less than or equal to upper bound. A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is an explicit or implicit contract with your users that includes consequences of meeting (or missing) the SLOs it contains. The distinguishing feature: if there are no explicit consequences for missing the targets, you are looking at an SLO, not an SLA.

## Categories of indicator

Different classes of service care about different indicators. User facing serving systems generally care about availability, latency, and throughput: can we respond to the request, how long did it take, and how many requests can be handled. Storage systems emphasize latency, availability, and durability: how long to read or write, can we access the data on demand, and is the data still there when we need it. Big data systems such as data processing pipelines care about throughput and end to end latency. Correctness is an attribute of interest for every system.

## Aggregation and percentiles

Most metrics are better thought of as distributions rather than averages. Averaging request latencies may seem attractive but obscures tail behavior: a small number of very slow requests can matter more than the mean. Using high order percentiles such as the 50th, 95th, 99th, and 99.9th reveals the long tail and the worst case that a fraction of users actually experience. The higher the variance in response times, the more the typical user experience is affected by the tail.

## Choosing targets

Five recommendations for choosing SLO targets: do not pick a target based on current performance, because current performance may require heroic effort to sustain; keep it simple, since complicated aggregations obscure changes; avoid absolutes such as infinitely scalable or always available; have as few SLOs as possible, just enough for good coverage; and do not make the SLO too tight too early, start loose and refine over time as you learn.

## Error budgets and the don't overachieve principle

Rather than requiring 100 percent, it is better to allow an error budget, a rate at which the SLOs can be missed, and track it on a daily or weekly basis. A key insight: users build on the reality of what you offer, rather than what you say you will supply, particularly for infrastructure services. If actual performance greatly exceeds the stated SLO, users come to depend on the higher level. In the Chubby lock service case study, dependent services assumed it would never go down, which created unsafe dependencies; Google deliberately triggered controlled outages to keep reliance in line with the published SLO. Do not overachieve: publish and defend a realistic level rather than an accidental one.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 3: Embracing Risk (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## 100 percent is the wrong target

SRE rejects the assumption that 100 percent reliability is desirable. Past a certain point increasing reliability is worse for a service and its users rather than better, because extreme reliability constrains how fast features can ship and raises cost disproportionately, while users usually cannot perceive the difference between very high reliability levels once their own devices and networks introduce failures. The right availability target is treated as both a minimum and a maximum.

## The cost of reliability

Cost does not increase linearly as reliability increments. Each additional nine of availability can cost roughly 100 times more than the previous one. Two cost dimensions matter: direct costs of redundant equipment and resources, and the opportunity cost of engineering capacity diverted from building user facing features.

## Measuring availability

Time based availability equals uptime over total time. A 99.99 percent target permits about 52.56 minutes of downtime per year. Aggregate availability, or request success rate, equals successful requests divided by total requests over a rolling window, which suits distributed systems where partial failure is normal. A service serving 2.5 million requests per day at 99.99 percent may fail up to 250 requests that day.

## The nines

Availability is quoted in nines: 99.9 percent is three nines, 99.99 percent is four nines, 99.999 percent is five nines. Each added nine is an order of magnitude closer to perfect.

## Risk tolerance

For consumer services the target depends on user expectations, competitive positioning, revenue impact, and whether the service is free or paid. Google Apps for Work targets 99.9 percent given enterprise dependence, while early YouTube in 2006 chose a lower target to prioritize rapid feature development. Infrastructure services with many clients use explicitly delineated levels of service: Bigtable offers low latency clusters with provisioned slack for reliability alongside throughput clusters run very hot at 10 to 50 percent of the cost. A cost benefit example: moving a $1M revenue service from 99.9 to 99.99 percent (a 0.09 percent gain) yields about $900 of value, so it is only worth doing if it costs less than $900.

## Error budgets

An error budget is one minus the availability target. For a 99.999 percent SLO the error budget is 0.001 percent of requests over the period. Product Management sets the SLO, monitoring measures actual uptime, and the difference is the remaining budget for the quarter; new releases proceed as long as measured uptime is above the SLO. Error budgets remove the politics from negotiations between product and SRE by giving both sides an objective, agreed metric. When the budget is nearly spent, product teams self regulate and raise testing rigor rather than needing SRE to enforce a freeze. Loosening an SLO increases the error budget and permits faster launches, aligning both teams on finding the right balance guided by measurement rather than politics, fear, or hope.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 5: Eliminating Toil (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## What toil is

Toil is the kind of work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly as a service grows. Toil is not simply work you do not like to do, and it is not the same as overhead. Overhead is administrative work such as meetings, HR paperwork, or expense reports; toil is operational work that directly keeps the service running.

## Six characteristics of toil

Work qualifies as toil to the degree it is: manual, requiring hands on human time even to run a script; repetitive, done again and again rather than a one time fix; automatable, meaning a machine could do it as well as a human; tactical, interrupt driven and reactive rather than strategy driven; without enduring value, leaving the service in the same state after it is done; and scaling linearly with service growth, so headcount would have to grow with traffic.

## The 50 percent target

Google SRE aims to keep each engineer's toil below 50 percent of their time, reserving the majority for engineering project work that reduces future toil or adds service features. Surveys put the actual average near 33 percent, with individuals ranging from 0 to 80 percent. A floor of toil exists because of on call and interrupts, roughly 25 to 33 percent depending on rotation size.

## Why toil is bad

Too much toil causes career stagnation, low morale, and attrition, and it slows progress because time spent on toil is time not spent engineering. It also creates confusion about the mission: SRE is an engineering organization, and behavior that treats it as a pure operations team erodes that identity. Excess toil can also normalize an unsustainable path where the team cannot keep up as the service grows. The remedy is to spend the engineering half of time on software and systems work that permanently removes toil, so a service can scale without a matching increase in operational load.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 6: Monitoring Distributed Systems, the Four Golden Signals (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## The Four Golden Signals

If you can measure only four metrics of your user facing system, focus on latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Latency is the time it takes to service a request; it is important to distinguish the latency of successful requests from the latency of failed requests, because a fast error can otherwise hide in the good latency numbers. Traffic is a measure of demand on the system, for example HTTP requests per second for a web service, network I/O rate, or concurrent sessions. Errors is the rate of requests that fail, either explicitly such as HTTP 500s, implicitly such as an HTTP 200 returned with the wrong content, or by policy such as any request slower than a committed threshold. Saturation is how full the service is, a measure of the fraction of the most constrained resource; many systems degrade in performance before they hit 100 percent utilization, so a utilization target is important.

## Why monitor

Monitoring exists to analyze long term trends, to compare over time and across experiments, to alert when something is broken or about to break, to build dashboards, and to conduct retrospective debugging. Good monitoring lets a system tell you when it is broken, or better, what is about to break.

## Symptoms versus causes

A monitoring system should address what is broken, the symptom, and why, the cause. The what versus why distinction is one of the most important in writing good monitoring with maximum signal and minimum noise. A user visible symptom (the website is slow) is separated from its cause (an overloaded database). Alert on symptoms that indicate real user impact.

## Black box and white box

White box monitoring is based on metrics exposed by the internals of the system, including logs and interfaces, and can detect imminent problems and failures masked by retries. Black box monitoring is symptom oriented and tests externally visible behavior as a user would see it, representing active, ongoing problems rather than predicted ones. A robust setup combines both.

## Alerting philosophy

When writing alerting rules, keep pages meaningful: every page should be urgent, actionable, and require intelligence, not a mechanical response. Pages that can be safely ignored are worse than no page because they train responders to ignore alerts. Symptoms that reflect definite user impact are better paging triggers than causes. Humans fatigue quickly, so a page must reflect a real, ongoing problem that only a human can address.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 15: Postmortem Culture, Learning from Failure (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## What a postmortem is

A postmortem is a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root cause or causes, and the follow up actions to prevent recurrence. Incidents and outages are inevitable given the scale and velocity of change, so the goal is to institutionalize learning from them rather than to avoid ever having them.

## Blameless postmortems

A blameless postmortem focuses on identifying the contributing causes of the incident without indicting any individual or team for bad or inappropriate behavior. It assumes that everyone involved had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had at the time. The mindset shifts from allocating blame to investigating the systematic reasons why an individual or team had incomplete or incorrect information. The core belief: you cannot fix people, but you can fix systems and processes to better support people making the right choices when designing and maintaining complex systems.

## Triggers

Common criteria that should trigger a postmortem include user visible downtime or degradation beyond a threshold, data loss of any kind, on call engineer intervention such as a rollback or diverting traffic, a resolution time above some threshold, and a monitoring failure that meant a problem was discovered by a human rather than by an alert. Teams agree these criteria in advance so postmortems are expected, not a punishment.

## Best practices

Remove blame so people have the confidence to escalate issues without fear. Do not stigmatize teams that file many postmortems; a high count reflects transparency, not incompetence. Ensure senior engineers review a postmortem before it is published, and share it broadly so the whole organization can learn. Visibly reward the people who do the work of writing effective postmortems and closing the follow up items. A postmortem that is filed but whose action items are never completed is of little value, so track the follow ups to completion.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 11: Being On-Call (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## Balanced on-call, by quantity and quality

Google caps operational load: SREs spend at least 50 percent of their time on engineering, and across the remainder no more than 25 percent is spent on call, leaving up to 25 percent for other operational work. Balance has two dimensions: quantity, the fraction of time spent on call, and quality, how many incidents occur during a shift.

## Team sizing

Because of the 25 percent on call ceiling, a single site team running a 24/7 rotation with a primary and a secondary needs a minimum of about eight engineers, so each person covers roughly one week per month. Multi site follow the sun rotations spread load across time zones and can reduce night shifts.

## Incident load target

Properly handling an incident, including root cause analysis, remediation, and writing the postmortem, takes about 6 hours. This leads to a hard limit of a maximum of 2 incidents per 12 hour on call shift. If a rotation regularly exceeds that, the service is generating too much operational load and the fix is to push work back to engineering and to the development team, not to absorb more toil.

## Response times

Response time expectations follow from the SLO. User facing or otherwise time critical services may require a response within about 5 minutes, while less sensitive services may allow 30 minutes. A service with a four nines availability target has roughly 13 minutes of downtime budget per quarter, which constrains how fast a page must be answered.

## Primary, secondary, and psychological safety

Rotations typically have a primary on call and a secondary; some teams use the secondary as a backstop for missed pages, others route non urgent work to the secondary. Key supports for on call resilience are clear escalation paths, well defined incident management procedures, and a blameless postmortem culture. Out of hours work should be compensated with time off in lieu or cash, capped as a proportion of salary, to reward participation without encouraging burnout.

title: DORA, The Four Keys and Software Delivery Performance Metrics
text:
## The metrics of software delivery performance

DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) measures software delivery performance with a small set of metrics that have grown from the original four keys. They divide into two groups: throughput, how quickly and how often change moves through the system, and stability or instability, how well those changes behave in production.

## Throughput metrics

Change lead time is the amount of time it takes for a change to go from committed to version control to deployed and running in production. Deployment frequency is the number of deployments over a given period, or equivalently the time between deployments. Failed deployment recovery time is the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention; this metric replaced the earlier time to restore service framing as the model matured.

## Stability metrics

Change fail rate is the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention (such as a hotfix, rollback, patch, or roll forward) following the deployment. Deployment rework rate, a newer signal, is the ratio of deployments that are unplanned and happen as a result of an incident in production.

## Why these metrics

Throughput and stability are not a tradeoff. The DORA research repeatedly finds that the highest performing teams do well on both at once: they ship small changes frequently with short lead times and also have low change failure rates and recover fast. Chasing speed by cutting quality, or chasing stability by slowing down, both tend to make the other worse. The four keys are outcome metrics: they are meant to be watched as a system and improved by investing in the underlying technical and cultural capabilities, not gamed individually.

title: Adam Wiggins (Heroku), The Twelve-Factor App
text:
## What the twelve-factor app is

The twelve-factor app is a methodology for building software as a service apps that use declarative formats for setup automation to minimize time and cost for new developers, have a clean contract with the underlying operating system for maximum portability, are suitable for deployment on modern cloud platforms, minimize divergence between development and production to enable continuous deployment, and can scale up without significant changes to tooling, architecture, or development practices. It is language and backing service agnostic.

## The twelve factors

I. Codebase: one codebase tracked in revision control, many deploys. II. Dependencies: explicitly declare and isolate dependencies, never relying on implicit system wide packages. III. Config: store config in the environment, strictly separated from code, so the same build can run in any environment. IV. Backing services: treat backing services such as databases, queues, and SMTP as attached resources reachable by a URL or locator in config, swappable without code changes. V. Build, release, run: strictly separate the build stage, the release stage that combines build with config, and the run stage; releases are immutable and can be rolled back. VI. Processes: execute the app as one or more stateless, share nothing processes; persistent data belongs in a stateful backing service. VII. Port binding: export services via port binding, the app is self contained and does not rely on runtime injection of a webserver. VIII. Concurrency: scale out via the process model, handling different workloads with different process types. IX. Disposability: maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown, so processes can be started or stopped at a moment's notice. X. Dev/prod parity: keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible, closing the time, personnel, and tools gaps to enable continuous deployment. XI. Logs: treat logs as event streams written unbuffered to stdout, leaving routing and storage to the execution environment. XII. Admin processes: run admin and management tasks such as migrations as one off processes in an identical environment to the long running processes.
